name: Pale Sky Blue
lede: Pale Sky Blue is a very light, slightly greenish blue; on screens it reads almost cyan, while painters have used the phrase for what finely ground azurite looks like.

sections.title: Two meanings
sections.body: The library lists the name in the xkcd color survey and in the ISCC-NBS system of 1955, block 184, with [[powder-blue]] the nearest named color at 4.8 units [1]. The swatch is cool and airy, a lightness of 93 of 100 [1]. Compare the more everyday [[sky-blue]].

sections.title: Sky blue from stone
sections.body:
Painters used the same words for a mineral blue. Ball says that very finely ground azurite develops a pale sky-blue with a hint of green, good for skies but less rich than the purple depth of ultramarine [2]. Coles agrees and adds the practical cost: the stone had to be pounded, then washed several times with fish glue, and a coarser grind gave a deeper blue that was gritty and translucent [3]. Ball ties this to a fifteenth-century Bolognese manuscript of recipes called *Segreti per Colori*, which lists various natural azures without clearly separating their mineral sources [2]. The mineral itself is the [[gem:azurite|azurite]] of the gem trade.

A painter's azurite sky is therefore greener and duller than this screen swatch, which is much closer to white.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: The swatch has a contrast of only 1.18 against white [1]. No painting in our archive of 23,781 has a color within six units of it covering at least five per cent of the canvas [4]. As photographed: museum photographs of aged, varnished paintings; a color match is not a pigment test.
